# Accessing Files

<!-- This file is generated by filen-cli. Do not edit it directly! -->

Commands name the files and directories in your Filen drive by their paths. A path that starts
with `/` starts at the root of the drive; any other path starts at the working directory: the
one `cd` went to in the REPL, or the one `--working-path` gives (`/` by default). `.` is the
directory a path is at and `..` its parent, so `cd ..` goes up one directory, and the root is
its own parent. Doubled and trailing slashes change nothing, but on the destination of `mv`
and `cp`: `mv a.txt docs/` moves `a.txt` into the existing directory `docs`, and fails if there
is none, where `mv a.txt docs` would rename `a.txt` to `docs`.

Quote a name that holds spaces, in your shell and in the REPL alike: `cat "my notes.txt"`.

`uuid:<UUID>` names the item with that UUID wherever it is, as `stat` and `ls -l --json` show
it: `stat uuid:<UUID>`. It is the only way to name an item whose name cannot be decrypted,
which listings show by its UUID in place of its name, and of an item below such a directory,
which no path leads to. Messages show an item without a path by its UUID, and an item put in a
directory without a path as `<name> in uuid:<UUID>`. Only `cd` needs a path, and refuses such
a directory; `mv`, `cp`, `edit`, `write` and `touch` need the name of the item itself. An item
in the trash is named this way in `trash-restore` and `trash-delete` only. Write a name that
starts with `uuid:` as `./uuid:...`.

`rm`, `mv`, `cp`, `cat`, `favorite` and `unfavorite` take several items, and a glob in the last
segment of a path: `*` matches any run of characters, `?` any one character and `[...]` one of
the characters in the brackets (`[a-z]` for a range, `[!...]` for one not in them). Names are
matched case-sensitively, and a name that starts with `.` only by a glob that does too. A glob
that matches nothing is an error, and an item whose name is exactly the glob is that item. Quote
globs so that your shell does not match them against your local files: `rm '/photos/*.tmp'`.
With several sources, the destination of `mv` and `cp` must be an existing directory. A command
given several items goes on past one it fails for, says why, and exits with code 1 at the end.

With `--json`, commands print JSON whose keys are the same everywhere. Sizes are in bytes,
dates are RFC 3339 strings in UTC, and a date an item lacks is `null`:
- `stat` prints a file as `{"name", "type": "file", "size", "modified", "created", "uuid"}`, a
  directory as `{"name", "type": "directory", "size", "files", "directories", "created",
  "color", "uuid"}`, and the drive (`stat /`) as `{"type": "drive", "usedStorage",
  "totalStorage", "files", "directories"}`. The old CLI's `mtimeMs` is now `modified`.
- `ls`, `ls -R`, `tree`, `list-trash`, `list-favorites` and `list-recents` print an array with
  an object per item: `{"name", "type", "created", "favorited", "uuid"}`, plus `"size"` and
  `"modified"` for a file and `"color"` for a directory. `ls -R` and `tree` add `"path"`, the
  path below the listed directory, and the listings of items from many directories
  (`list-favorites`, `list-recents`) the absolute `"path"`, which is `null` when it cannot be
  found out. An empty listing is `[]`.
- `list-public-links` prints an array with an object per link instead: `{"path", "type",
  "uuid", "linkUuid", "expiresAt", "url"}`, where `"expiresAt"` is `null` for a link that never
  expires.
- `search` prints `{"results": [{"path", "type", "size", "uuid"}], "total", "complete"}`.
- `du` prints `{"path", "size", "items": [{"name", "type", "size"}]}`, `versions` an array of
  `{"uuid", "timestamp", "size", "current"}`, `cat`, `head` and `tail` `{"text"}`, `pwd`
  `{"path"}`, and `view` and `drive` `{"url"}`.

> `cd <DIRECTORY>`  
> Change the working directory (in REPL)  
> 🠊 `<DIRECTORY>` Directory to navigate into (supports "..")

> `pwd`  
> Print the working directory

> `ls [OPTIONS] [DIRECTORY]`  
> List files in a directory  
> 🠊 `[DIRECTORY]` Directory to list files in, or a file to show (default: the current working directory)  
> 🠊 `-l, --long` Use a long listing format: sizes, modification dates (creation dates of directories), [color] after colored directories and (*) after favorited items  
> 🠊 `-R, --recursive` List everything below the directory, one path relative to it per line, each directory followed by what it holds

> `tree [DIRECTORY]`  
> Draw everything below a directory as a tree (with --json: the listing of ls -R --json)  
> 🠊 `[DIRECTORY]` Directory to draw (default: the current working directory)

> `du [OPTIONS] [FILE_OR_DIRECTORY]`  
> Show the size of each item in a directory, a directory's being that of every file below it, and the total  
> 🠊 `[FILE_OR_DIRECTORY]` Directory or file to show the size of (default: the current working directory)  
> 🠊 `-s, --summarize` Show only the total

> `cat <FILES>...`  
> Print the contents of files as the bytes they hold, one after the other (with --json: {"text": ...}, for UTF-8 text only)  
> 🠊 `<FILES>...` Files to print, or globs such as '*.txt' (quoted)

> `head [OPTIONS] <FILE>`  
> Print the first lines of a file as the bytes they hold (with --json: {"text": ...})  
> 🠊 `<FILE>` File to print  
> 🠊 `-n, --lines <LINES>` Number of lines to print [default: 10]

> `tail [OPTIONS] <FILE>`  
> Print the last lines of a file as the bytes they hold (with --json: {"text": ...})  
> 🠊 `<FILE>` File to print  
> 🠊 `-n, --lines <LINES>` Number of lines to print [default: 10]

> `stat <FILE_OR_DIRECTORY>`  
> Show information about a file, a directory or the Filen drive  
> 🠊 `<FILE_OR_DIRECTORY>` File or directory to show information about ("/" for the Filen drive)

> `open <FILE>`  
> Open a file in the app your system opens its type with, from a local copy that is kept  
> 🠊 `<FILE>` File to open

> `edit <FILE>`  
> Edit a local copy of a file in $VISUAL, $EDITOR or the app your system opens its type with, then upload your changes as a new version (kept locally instead if the file changed meanwhile)  
> 🠊 `<FILE>` File to edit

> `view [OPTIONS] [FILE_OR_DIRECTORY]`  
> Print the web drive's URL of a directory, or of a file's directory, and open it in the browser  
> 🠊 `[FILE_OR_DIRECTORY]` File or directory to view (default: the current working directory)  
> 🠊 `--no-open` Only print the URL

> `drive [OPTIONS]`  
> Print the web drive's URL and open it in the browser  
> 🠊 `--no-open` Only print the URL

`search <query>` prints every file and directory under the working directory (or
`--working-path`), at any depth, whose name contains the query, ignoring case. Names and the
query are compared in Unicode NFC, and spaces around the query are ignored. It prints one full
path per line, directories first, or with `--json`
`{"results": [{"path", "type", "size", "uuid"}], "total", "complete"}`, where only files have a
`size`.

The search reads a local cache of your drive, which it brings up to date first. If that takes
longer than 30 seconds, it prints what the cache holds and warns that the results may be
incomplete (`"complete": false` with `--json`).

Without a query, `search` is interactive in a terminal: results appear as you type, and
choosing one goes to that directory, or to the directory of that file.

> `search [OPTIONS] [QUERY]`  
> Search for files and directories by name  
> 🠊 `[QUERY]` Part of the names to look for, matched ignoring case (without it, search interactively)  
> 🠊 `--type <TYPE>` Only list files, or only directories [possible values: file, dir]  
> 🠊 `--limit <LIMIT>` Print at most this many results [default: 100000]

> `mkdir [OPTIONS] <DIRECTORY>`  
> Create a new directory  
> 🠊 `<DIRECTORY>` Directory to create  
> 🠊 `-r, --recursive` Recursively create parent directories

> `rm [OPTIONS] <FILES_OR_DIRECTORIES>...`  
> Remove files or directories  
> 🠊 `<FILES_OR_DIRECTORIES>...` Files or directories to remove, or globs such as '*.txt' (quoted)  
> 🠊 `-p, --permanent` Permanently delete the files or directories, asking first unless --yes is given (default: move to trash)

> `write <FILE> [CONTENT]...`  
> Write text to a file, creating it or replacing its content  
> 🠊 `<FILE>` File to write to  
> 🠊 `[CONTENT]...` Text to write, its words joined by spaces (default: what stdin reads when it is not a terminal, otherwise nothing)

> `touch <FILE>`  
> Create an empty file, or set the modification date of an existing one to now  
> 🠊 `<FILE>` File to create or touch

> `mv <SOURCES>... <DESTINATION>`  
> Move and/or rename files or directories  
> 🠊 `<SOURCES>...` Files or directories to move, or globs such as '*.txt' (quoted)  
> 🠊 `<DESTINATION>` Destination: an existing directory to move the sources into, or, for one source, its new path (to move and/or rename it)

> `cp <SOURCES>... <DESTINATION>`  
> Copy files or directories  
> 🠊 `<SOURCES>...` Files or directories to copy, or globs such as '*.txt' (quoted)  
> 🠊 `<DESTINATION>` Destination: an existing directory to copy the sources into, or, for one source, the path of the copy (to copy it under a new name)

> `versions [OPTIONS] <FILE>`  
> List the versions of a file, newest first, or restore or delete one of them  
> 🠊 `<FILE>` File whose versions to list  
> 🠊 `--restore <VERSION>` Restore the version with this UUID, making it the file's current content  
> 🠊 `--delete <VERSION>` Permanently delete the version with this UUID, asking first unless --yes is given

> `list-favorites`  
> List favorited items

> `favorite <FILES_OR_DIRECTORIES>...`  
> Favorite files or directories  
> 🠊 `<FILES_OR_DIRECTORIES>...` Files or directories to favorite, or globs such as '*.txt' (quoted)

> `unfavorite <FILES_OR_DIRECTORIES>...`  
> Unfavorite files or directories  
> 🠊 `<FILES_OR_DIRECTORIES>...` Files or directories to unfavorite, or globs such as '*.txt' (quoted)

> `color <DIRECTORY> <COLOR>`  
> Set the color of a directory  
> 🠊 `<DIRECTORY>` Directory to color  
> 🠊 `<COLOR>` The color: default, blue, green, purple, red, gray, or a hex color like #85bcff

> `list-recents`  
> List recently accessed items

> `list-trash [OPTIONS]`  
> List trashed items  
> 🠊 `-l, --long` Use a long listing format: sizes, modification dates (creation dates of directories), [color] after colored directories and (*) after favorited items

> `trash-restore [OPTIONS] [ITEMS]...`  
> Restore trashed items  
> 🠊 `[ITEMS]...` Trashed items by name, or by UUID when several share a name (default: pick one interactively)  
> 🠊 `--all` Restore every trashed item

> `trash-delete [OPTIONS] [ITEMS]...`  
> Permanently delete trashed items, asking first unless --yes is given  
> 🠊 `[ITEMS]...` Trashed items by name, or by UUID when several share a name (default: pick one interactively)  
> 🠊 `--all` Permanently delete every trashed item

> `empty-trash`  
> Permanently delete all trashed items, asking first unless --yes is given

`public-link <path>` shows the public link of a file or directory: its settings, when it
expires (UTC) if it does, and its URL, the address to share. `list-public-links` lists the path,
expiry (UTC, or "never") and URL of every linked item (with `--json`, also each link's
`linkUuid`, and its expiry as `expiresAt`, `null` for a link that never expires).

In a terminal, `public-link` offers to edit or delete an existing link, and asks for a new
link's settings: when it expires, a password, and whether the item can be downloaded. The link
is created as soon as its settings are confirmed, and its URL is printed then. A new link is
created with the default settings (no password, never expires, downloadable) and then given its
own; if that fails and they would have protected the item more, with a password, an expiry or
downloads off, the link is deleted again rather than left open. Press Esc to
cancel a prompt, which creates and changes nothing. `--yes` answers "Enable download?" with yes,
as it answers every yes/no question, so editing a link without downloads turns them on, which it
says on stderr (`--no-download` keeps them off); the other settings are still asked. Without a
terminal to
prompt on (or with `--no-input`), `public-link` only prints an existing link, and fails with
exit code 2 instead of creating a missing one: the setting options below create it without
prompting.

The options do the same without prompting. `--expires <never|1h|6h|1d|3d|7d|14d|30d>`,
`--password <PASSWORD>` or `--no-password`, and `--download` or `--no-download` create the link
if there is none, and change only the settings given. `--show` prints the link and changes
nothing. `--delete` deletes it after asking to confirm, which `--yes` answers.

A password given with `--password` is part of the command line, so your shell saves it in its
history, and other users of the computer can see it while the command runs. The CLI never reads
a link password from the environment: to keep one out of the history, enter it at the prompt.

> `list-public-links`  
> List public links, with the path and URL of each linked file or directory

> `public-link [OPTIONS] <FILE_OR_DIRECTORY>`  
> Create, update or delete a public link for a file or directory
>
> Without options, it shows the link and offers to edit or delete it, or asks for a new link's settings. With a setting option, it creates the link if there is none and changes only the settings given.  
> 🠊 `<FILE_OR_DIRECTORY>` File or directory to create, update or delete a public link for  
> 🠊 `--password <PASSWORD>` Protect the link with this password. It is read from the command line only, so it ends up in your shell's history  
> 🠊 `--no-password` Remove the link's password  
> 🠊 `--expires <EXPIRATION>` When the link expires [possible values: never, 1h, 6h, 1d, 3d, 7d, 14d, 30d]  
> 🠊 `--download` Allow downloading the linked item  
> 🠊 `--no-download` Do not allow downloading the linked item  
> 🠊 `--show` Print the link's settings and URL, and change nothing  
> 🠊 `--delete` Delete the link (asks to confirm, which --yes answers)
